title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Introduction
content: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary and stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. [1] ACTH is clinically important because it regulates cortisol production, a hormone with broad physiologic effects, including suppression of inflammation, stimulation of metabolic activity, and elevation of blood glucose, which are critical components of the stress response. [2] Dysregulation of ACTH activity is associated with disorders such as Cushing syndrome and primary adrenal insufficiency.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Introduction
content: A thorough understanding of ACTH physiology is essential for accurate diagnosis and management of disorders affecting cortisol regulation. Insight into ACTH dynamics enables clinicians to identify underlying pathologies, tailor therapeutic strategies, and anticipate complications arising from dysregulated cortisol levels.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Cellular Level
content: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) is a large precursor molecule cleaved within corticotroph cells to generate several peptides, including ACTH. [3] ACTH is a 39-amino acid peptide hormone. [4] ACTH activates the adrenocortical pathway after release from the anterior pituitary, initiating cholesterol conversion to cortisol via the steroidogenic pathway. The binding of ACTH to G protein-coupled receptors raises intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), triggering enzymatic cascades that culminate in cortisol secretion. [5]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Function
content: The principal function of ACTH is the stimulation of the steroidogenic pathway in the adrenal cortex. ACTH regulates the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis, where cortisol and adrenal androgens are produced, respectively. [6] [7] Cortisol exerts wide-ranging physiologic effects, including enhancement of metabolic activity leading to elevated blood glucose and free fatty acid levels, suppression of the inflammatory and immune responses, and increased cardiac output and vasoconstriction. [8] Cortisol production is particularly critical during stress. Following activation of the sympathetic nervous system, the HPA axis augments cortisol synthesis, sustaining the stress response through these mechanisms. [9] Persistent HPA axis activation in the setting of chronic stress may contribute to adverse health outcomes.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Function
content: ACTH also regulates adrenal androgen synthesis. Dihydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and androstenedione, precursors of sex steroids, are primarily controlled by ACTH. Although ACTH can influence mineralocorticoid secretion, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system serves as the primary regulator of this pathway. [10]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Mechanism
content: The hypothalamus, located in the ventral brain, secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which stimulates ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary. ACTH then acts on the adrenal cortex to promote cortisol synthesis and release. ACTH secretion follows a diurnal rhythm, peaking in the early morning before awakening and declining gradually throughout the day. This pattern is disrupted in Cushing disease, with ACTH levels remaining elevated at night. [11]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Mechanism
content: The HPA axis is regulated by negative feedback, in which elevated cortisol suppresses ACTH and CRH secretion, thereby limiting further cortisol production. Conversely, low cortisol levels stimulate ACTH and CRH release, increasing cortisol synthesis.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Pathophysiology
content: Disorders associated with ACTH secretion may be classified by simultaneously evaluating cortisol and ACTH levels. Low cortisol with elevated ACTH suggests primary adrenal insufficiency, whereas low cortisol with low ACTH indicates secondary or tertiary adrenal insufficiency. When cortisol is elevated, measurement of ACTH distinguishes between ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent causes. Elevated cortisol with elevated ACTH suggests ACTH hypersecretion due to a pituitary adenoma, as in Cushing disease, or an ectopic ACTH-producing tumor. Elevated cortisol with suppressed ACTH indicates autonomous cortisol production by an adrenal lesion, with feedback inhibition of pituitary ACTH secretion.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Cushing syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by excessive cortisol production. [12] Classification is based on ACTH dependence. ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome results from pituitary ACTH hypersecretion, termed "Cushing disease," or ectopic ACTH production by nonpituitary tumors, both of which drive cortisol overproduction. In contrast, ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome arises from exogenous glucocorticoid administration or autonomous cortisol secretion by an adrenal adenoma. [13] The term "Cushing syndrome" encompasses all causes of cortisol excess, whereas Cushing disease specifically denotes pituitary ACTH overproduction.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Cushing syndrome manifests with a broad spectrum of clinical features. Key signs that increase the likelihood of this diagnosis include facial plethora, violaceous striae, easy bruising, a rounded facial appearance (“moon face”), central adiposity, and proximal muscle weakness. Additional manifestations may include depression, impaired skin healing, insomnia, acne, osteopenia, decreased libido, weight gain, dorsocervical fat accumulation (“buffalo hump”), and hirsutism.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Evaluation of Cushing syndrome requires a systematic approach. Clinical history should focus on identifying exogenous glucocorticoid use, which can contribute to hypercortisolism. In cases of exogenous steroid exposure, gradual dose reduction under close clinical monitoring is necessary to prevent adrenal insufficiency. [14]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Initial evaluation of Cushing syndrome involves 1 of several tests: urine-free cortisol measurement, the 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or late-night salivary cortisol assessment. [15] Late-night salivary cortisol requires the collection of 2 samples on consecutive nights between 11 pm and 1 am, with precise labeling of collection times. Cortisol and ACTH normally follow a diurnal rhythm, resulting in low salivary cortisol levels at night. This rhythm is disrupted in Cushing syndrome, and nighttime cortisol levels remain elevated. [16]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: The 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test involves taking 1 mg of dexamethasone orally, typically between 11 pm and midnight, followed by measuring serum cortisol the next morning between 8 and 9 am. Dexamethasone suppresses ACTH secretion in individuals with normal glucocorticoid regulation, producing low serum cortisol levels. In contrast, patients with autonomous glucocorticoid overproduction demonstrate absent or inadequate suppression of ACTH and cortisol.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Positive results from initial testing, or negative results in patients with high clinical suspicion of hypercortisolism, warrant referral to a specialist endocrinology service for comprehensive evaluation. Concurrent assessment should exclude other physiologic causes of elevated cortisol, including pregnancy, depression, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and significant obesity.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: Following confirmation of Cushing syndrome, differentiation between ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent forms requires measurement of serum ACTH. Elevated or high-normal ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, whereas suppressed ACTH identifies ACTH-independent disease. [17]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome arises from either Cushing disease, caused by a pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH, or ectopic ACTH production. Differentiation between these etiologies relies on diagnostic procedures such as the high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, desmopressin stimulation test, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS). [18] Magnetic resonance imaging is frequently employed to identify pituitary adenomas responsible for Cushing disease. For ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, obtaining a computed tomography (CT) scan of the adrenal glands after excluding exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can confirm the presence of adrenal tumors.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: First-line management of Cushing syndrome involves surgical resection of the tumor when it is visible on imaging and considered resectable. Transsphenoidal surgery is the preferred approach in Cushing disease. [19]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Cushing Syndrome
content: When surgery is not feasible or the tumor recurs, alternative therapeutic strategies include repeat transsphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy for residual or recurrent pituitary tumors—often as adjuvant therapy—and medical treatment with steroidogenesis inhibitors such as metyrapone, ketoconazole, and osilodrostat. Novel pharmacologic agents, including the 11-β-hydroxylase inhibitor osilodrostat and the glucocorticoid receptor antagonist mifepristone, have been increasingly employed. [20] [21] [22]

content: Bilateral adrenalectomy is indicated in severe hypercortisolism requiring urgent control or disease refractory to other interventions. Postoperative management necessitates lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement therapy. [23]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Ectopic Adrenocorticotropic Hormone Syndrome
content: Ectopic ACTH syndrome arises from excessive ACTH production by nonpituitary tumors, most commonly neuroendocrine neoplasms of the thorax, with small-cell lung cancer representing the most frequent cause. Clinical presentation typically involves a rapidly developing hypercortisolism over several weeks, with manifestations similar to those observed in Cushing syndrome. Additional features often include hypokalemia and treatment-resistant hypertension.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Ectopic Adrenocorticotropic Hormone Syndrome
content: Evaluation of suspected ectopic ACTH syndrome focuses on identifying the causative tumor. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and neck is generally recommended, with positron emission tomography considered when further localization is necessary. Definitive management involves surgical excision of the tumor when it is identifiable on imaging and metastasis has been excluded. Radiotherapy may be employed in cases of metastatic or unresectable tumors. Medical therapies and, in selected cases, bilateral adrenalectomy can serve as adjunctive or alternative interventions.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
content: Primary adrenal insufficiency is a rare disorder resulting from inadequate production of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, or both. [24] Multiple etiologies exist, with autoimmune adrenalitis, known as Addison disease, representing the most common cause in Western populations. [25] Clinical presentation often involves nonspecific symptoms such as malaise, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss, which may develop either acutely or gradually over several weeks to months. Hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes may also be observed.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
content: The corticotropin stimulation test, also known as the short Synacthen test, serves as the standard diagnostic tool for adrenal insufficiency. Administration of 250 mcg of intravenous corticotropin is followed by measurement of plasma ACTH and cortisol levels at baseline, 30 minutes, and 60 minutes. Historically, cortisol levels below 18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L) were considered diagnostic, although thresholds varied with assay methodology. More recent studies support the use of lower cutoffs of 14 to 15 mcg/dL (approximately 400 nmol/L) for diagnosis. [26] Plasma ACTH exceeding twice the upper limit of normal also supports a diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency.

content: Electrolyte abnormalities, including hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia, are frequently observed in affected patients. [27] Screening for other autoimmune disorders is recommended, as patients with Addison disease often present with concomitant autoimmune conditions.

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
content: Acute presentations of primary adrenal insufficiency require immediate intervention, even before biochemical confirmation. Management includes aggressive resuscitation with intravenous fluids to address severe volume depletion and intravenous glucocorticoid replacement, typically with hydrocortisone. [28]

title: Physiology, Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) -- Clinical Significance -- Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
content: Long-term management of primary adrenal insufficiency necessitates lifelong glucocorticoid replacement, with fludrocortisone supplementation for patients with aldosterone deficiency. Hydrocortisone is preferred for glucocorticoid therapy, usually administered in 3 divided doses per day, with the highest dose in the morning to replicate physiological circadian variation. Mineralocorticoid replacement is commonly achieved with fludrocortisone. Patients should be provided with an emergency steroid card to inform healthcare personnel of chronic steroid therapy and receive counselling regarding "sick day rules," including doubling the hydrocortisone dose during periods of acute illness. [29]
